title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns: Basic Patterns
summary: Distinguish nouns that can be counted from nouns treated as a mass or substance. Choose singular or plural forms, articles, some and any, and quantity expressions such as many, much, a few and a little.
learningObjectives: Identify singular and plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns in everyday contexts.
Choose an appropriate article or determiner for a singular countable noun, and avoid a/an directly before an uncountable noun.
Use some and any naturally with plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns.
Match many and a few with countable plurals, and much and a little with uncountable nouns.

explanation.heading: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms
explanation.body: A countable noun identifies an item that can be counted separately. It can be singular or plural: one camera, three cameras. A singular countable noun normally needs an article or another determiner in a complete noun phrase. In statements about a whole category, a bare plural is common.
explanation.example: The studio owns four cameras, and cameras need regular cleaning.

explanation.heading: Uncountable nouns describe substances and abstract quantities
explanation.body: Many materials, substances and general activities are normally uncountable. These nouns do not take an ordinary plural ending when they refer to a mass: water, flour, music, electricity and luck. They can be used without an article when speaking generally. A singular verb is normally used when the uncountable noun is the subject.
explanation.example: Fresh water is available near the entrance.

explanation.heading: Choose articles and measurable units
explanation.body: Use a/an with a singular countable noun when it is appropriate: a ticket, an umbrella. Do not attach a/an directly to an uncountable mass noun: not a flour or a music. To identify a countable portion, add a unit such as a bag of flour, a glass of water or a piece of equipment.
explanation.example: We bought an umbrella and a large bottle of water.

explanation.heading: Some and any work with plurals and mass nouns
explanation.body: Some and any can refer both to an unspecified number of countable items and an unspecified amount of uncountable material. Some is common in affirmative statements; any is common in questions and negatives. These are common tendencies, not absolute rules: offers and requests often use some.
explanation.example: We have some chairs, but we do not have any spare tables.

explanation.heading: Many/few and much/little measure different kinds of quantity
explanation.body: Use many and (a) few with plural countable nouns; use much and (a) little with uncountable nouns. A few and a little both express a positive, though small, quantity; few and little without a sound more negative. Much is particularly common in negatives and questions; a lot of works with both types in many everyday statements.
explanation.example: We have a few minutes, but we do not have much time.

comparisons.title: Individual objects versus an uncountable substance

left.label: Countable objects
left.example: There are six cups on the shelf.
left.note: Cups are separate objects and take a plural form after six.

right.label: Uncountable substance
right.example: There is some water in the jug.
right.note: Water is treated as a mass and takes a singular verb here.

comparisons.title: Different quantity words for different noun types

left.label: Plural countable
left.example: We have a few spare tickets.
left.note: A few modifies the plural countable noun tickets.

right.label: Uncountable
right.example: We have a little spare time.
right.note: A little modifies the uncountable noun time.

examples.sentence: An electrician checked the faulty sockets.
examples.note: Electrician is a singular countable noun and takes an; sockets is plural.

examples.sentence: Most people enjoy music while travelling.
examples.note: Music is uncountable in this general sense and appears without a/an.

examples.sentence: We received some messages before the meeting.
examples.note: Some modifies the countable plural messages.

examples.sentence: There is not much petrol in the tank.
examples.note: Much modifies the uncountable noun petrol.

examples.sentence: Only a few students arrived early for the workshop.
examples.note: A few describes a small but positive number of countable students.

commonMistakes.why: A countable noun after a number greater than one needs a plural form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: They asked for an equipment to record the event.
commonMistakes.correct: They asked for equipment to record the event.
commonMistakes.why: Equipment is uncountable, so it does not take an directly.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We heard a beautiful music from upstairs.
commonMistakes.correct: We heard beautiful music from upstairs.
commonMistakes.why: Music is uncountable in this sense and does not take a directly.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There are a little seats left near the front.
commonMistakes.correct: There are a few seats left near the front.
commonMistakes.why: Seats is plural and countable, so use a few rather than a little.

studyTips: Classify a noun as separate items or a mass before choosing its article, number and quantifier.
Make two columns for many/a few and much/a little; add your own nouns to each column and read the combinations aloud.
When you want to count an uncountable substance, name the unit: a glass of juice, three bags of flour or two pieces of equipment.

exercises.prompt: For the training course, I need ___ notebook to record my observations.
exercises.feedback: Notebook is a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound, so a is required here.

exercises.prompt: There is not ___ water left in the container.
exercises.feedback: Water is uncountable; much is natural in negative quantity statements.

exercises.prompt: There are still ___ empty chairs at the back of the room.
exercises.feedback: Chairs is a plural countable noun, so a few expresses a small number.

exercises.prompt: We do not need ___ flour for this small cake.
exercises.feedback: Flour is a mass noun, so use much after do not need.

exercises.prompt: The studio has three ___ (camera). Write the correct plural noun.
exercises.feedback: Three requires the plural form cameras.

exercises.prompt: The organisers sent us ___ (information). Use some + the uncountable noun.
exercises.feedback: Some information is grammatical; information is uncountable here.

exercises.prompt: Mira is ___ (architect). Write the correct indefinite article and noun.
exercises.feedback: Architect begins with a vowel sound and is a singular countable noun, so use an architect.

exercises.prompt: There is ___ (work) left before the exhibition opens. Use a little + the noun.
exercises.feedback: A little modifies the uncountable noun work.

exercises.prompt: Add only the missing indefinite article a/an: She ordered new laptop for the office.
acceptedAnswers: She ordered a new laptop for the office.
exercises.feedback: A singular countable noun such as laptop needs an appropriate determiner; the required indefinite article here is a.

exercises.prompt: Correct the quantity word only: There is not many milk left in the fridge.
acceptedAnswers: There is not much milk left in the fridge.
exercises.feedback: Milk is uncountable, so much replaces many.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the noun ending: There are five book on the desk.
acceptedAnswers: There are five books on the desk.
exercises.feedback: A number greater than one requires the countable plural books.

exercises.prompt: Remove the unnecessary article only: A music was playing quietly in the shop.
acceptedAnswers: Music was playing quietly in the shop.
exercises.feedback: Music is uncountable here, so it does not take a before the noun.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence using these exact facts: the office; have; four printers. Begin “The office has”.
Say one sentence using these facts: we; need; an umbrella. Begin “We need”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Umbrella is a singular countable noun that takes an.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one negative sentence using the exact words “I”, “do not”, “have”, “much” and “time”. End with “today”.
acceptedAnswers: I do not have much time today.
speakingExercises.feedback: Much is used with the uncountable noun time.

speakingExercises.prompt: Answer in one full sentence. Question: What is in the jar? Given fact: there is some sugar in the jar. Begin “There is”.
acceptedAnswers: There is some sugar in the jar.
speakingExercises.feedback: Some sugar is natural because sugar is uncountable here.

speakingExercises.prompt: Rephrase “The team has a small number of spare chairs”. Begin “The team has a few” and end “spare chairs”.
acceptedAnswers: The team has a few spare chairs.
speakingExercises.feedback: A few is used with the plural countable noun chairs.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say a complete question. Use these facts: any / batteries / in / the drawer. Begin “Are there”.
acceptedAnswers: Are there any batteries in the drawer?
speakingExercises.feedback: Any can modify a plural countable noun in a question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences from these facts. First: the children / have / three books. Second: they / need / some paper. Use these words in this order and do not add details.
acceptedAnswers: The children have three books. They need some paper.
speakingExercises.feedback: Books takes a plural ending after three; paper is uncountable as a writing material.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks whether the studio has any spare space. Give one negative sentence with the exact phrase “not much room”. Begin “There is”.
speakingExercises.feedback: Room means space here and takes much, not many.

listeningExercises.audioText: For the celebration, Marta packed four candles and some ribbon, but she forgot the matches.
listeningExercises.feedback: She packed four candles and some ribbon, but forgot the matches.

listeningExercises.audioText: We already have six eggs, but there is no flour left for the cake.
listeningExercises.prompt: What ingredient do they still need?
listeningExercises.feedback: No flour left means they need flour; the six eggs are already available.

listeningExercises.audioText: The school library has some new magazines on the entrance table.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word noun phrase immediately after “has” in the recording.
listeningExercises.feedback: Some new magazines is a plural noun phrase; some refers to an unspecified number.

listeningExercises.audioText: There are plenty of free desks, but there is very little storage space behind the counter.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very little describes the small amount of uncountable storage space.

listeningExercises.audioText: I brought an umbrella on the walk, but I did not bring any drinking water.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which thing did the speaker not bring?
listeningExercises.feedback: Did not bring any drinking water states the missing item.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have very little fuel left, so we need to stop at a petrol station soon.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why do the travellers need to stop?
listeningExercises.feedback: Very little fuel left explains why they need a petrol station.

listeningExercises.audioText: There are a few questions that the visitors want to ask before the tour.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression immediately after “are”.
listeningExercises.feedback: A few modifies the plural countable noun questions.

listeningExercises.audioText: We do not have much time before the doors close, so please hurry.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single quantity word immediately after “have”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Much modifies the uncountable noun time.
